entries.title: No, this arm
entries.body:
I was showing a small cuttlefish how to disappear against the weed. I raised an arm to point out the useful bits. He raised an arm too.

I lowered myself. So did he. I made a rough patch along my back. He concentrated very hard and raised the arm higher.

After a while I realised he thought the raised arm was making us invisible.

I put mine down. He looked absolutely betrayed.

We stayed like that until a fish passed. He vanished beautifully against the weed. One small arm remained in plain sight.

I did not correct him while the fish was there. I was busy putting mine back up.

image.title: File:Sepia común (Sepia officinalis), Parque natural de la Arrábida, Portugal, 2020-07-21, DD 62.jpg
image.creator: Diego Delso
image.description: Common cuttlefish (Sepia officinalis), Arrábida National Park, Portugal. The common cuttlefish is one of the largest and best-known cuttlefish species. They are a migratory species that spend the summer and spring inshore for spawning and then move to depths of 100 to 200m during autumn and winter. They only have a lifespan of 1–2 years and have many predators including sharks, dolphins, seals, fish, and cephalopods which includes other cuttlefish. During the day, most cuttlefish can be found buried below the substrate and fairly inactive. At night however, they are actively searching for prey and can ambush them from under the substrate. Cuttlefish are carnivorous and eat a variety of organisms including crustaceans (crabs and shrimp), small fish, molluscs (clams and snails), and sometimes other cuttlefish.

entries.title: The bit underneath
entries.body:
The wrasse found me beside a stone and asked whether I was going to move.

I told him I'd had a horrible morning. He waited. I told him the rest of it, including the bit where I had been horrible back. He kept waiting.

Eventually I said it was kind of him to listen.

He said there might be something under me.

I moved. He ate whatever it was, then came back.

I asked whether there was something under me now.

No, he said. What happened after you said that?

entries.title: Under the enormous one
entries.body:
A little fish tucked himself beneath me and told another little fish there was room.

I said I wasn't a rock.

He said he knew. Rocks didn't follow you.

I had not meant to follow him. I'd moved a little when he moved, then a little more. There was quite a lot of bare water ahead of him.

The second fish came under. Someone brushed my belly. I tried to keep still without looking as though I was trying.

When they came out at the weed, one said thank you to the enormous cuttlefish.

I had been feeling enormous all morning. I let him say it twice.

entries.title: I heard you the first time
entries.body:
I made myself part of the rock because I didn't want to speak to anyone. The wrasse came by and called my name.

I kept still.

He called again, much louder. I let the rough bits along my back rise. He went around the other side and called there.

This was exactly the sort of attention I had been hoping to avoid. It was also becoming important that he not leave.

I moved one eye.

He said he'd seen that. I said it could have been anything.

He settled beside the rock. After a while he asked if anything was hungry.

A small, extremely local part of the rock said yes.

entries.title: The short walk
entries.body:
I went for a walk without bringing anything back to improve the entrance.

There was an excellent stone. I examined it. One side was flat. I could already feel where it would go.

I left it.

Farther along, I found a better one. I left that too. By the time I turned around I was in a foul mood and the bottom was covered in things I had heroically failed to pick up.

At home I went straight inside. Nothing caught. Nothing needed moving.

I came out again to check I was at the right hole.

entries.title: Don't make me say it loudly
entries.body:
After the molt, she left food outside. She didn't call into the hole or ask whether I was feeling strong yet.

I waited until she was gone to take it.

The next time I waited less. By the fourth visit, my armor had hardened and I could have gone out myself. I stayed near the entrance instead.

She put the food down and said this was the last one. I said that was fine. I had been perfectly capable yesterday.

She picked it back up.

I came a little farther out.

I said yesterday had been nice.

image.title: File:Camarón mantis (Odontodactylus scyllarus), Anilao, Filipinas, 2023-08-24, DD 164.jpg
image.creator: Diego Delso
image.description: This species ranges in size from 3–18 centimetres (1.2–7.1 in) and is a burrower, constructing U-shaped holes in the loose substrate near the bases of coral reefs in water ranging from 3–40 metres (9.8–131.2 ft). It's a smasher, with club-shaped raptorial appendages. An agile and active intertidal and sub-intertidal predator, it prefers gastropods, crustaceans, and bivalves, and will repeatedly deliver blunt force to the exoskeleton of its prey until it can gain access to the underlying soft tissue for consumption. It is reported to have a "punch" of over 80 km/h (50 miles/h), the fastest recorded punch of any living animal. The acceleration is similar to that in a .22 LR bullet fired from a handgun.

entries.title: You go first
entries.body:
We met on the narrow strip of sand between the rocks. He stopped. I stopped.

I moved to let him through. He moved the same way. We corrected together. Then we did it again.

For a moment I was furious. I had been unmistakably considerate. He was making it look like a threat.

He backed up and lowered himself. I realised he was frightened.

I went around the rock. The long way, out of sight, where he couldn't mistake it for anything.

When I reached the other side he was there, having gone around to let me pass.

We stared at each other. Then he laughed. It was the first noise either of us had made.
